---
title: Plugins and the toolkit
description: A plugin is one file with no imports and no build step. How they load and what they get.
sidebar: { order: 4 }
---

A plugin is an integration, the same shape as the built-in ones, packaged as a single file.

:::caution[Plugins run as Valet]
A plugin has the same access as a built-in, including the keys you give it. Its cards are checked, and its code isn't sandboxed. Install only what you trust, and read it first: it's one file.
:::

## Install one

1. Put the file in `data/integrations/`. With Docker, that's the `./data` folder you mounted.
2. Add its block under `integrations:`, with the `type:` the plugin declares. Place its widgets in the layout as usual. Secrets go in `.env`.
3. Restart Valet. Editing the file doesn't reload it. The log lists what loaded, and why anything was skipped.

Every `.js` and `.mjs` file in that folder loads, in name order.

From source, you can also install from npm and list the package:

```yaml title="config.yaml"
plugins: [valet-integration-something]
```

A built-in type can't be replaced unless the config says so:

```yaml title="config.yaml"
plugins:
  packages: [valet-integration-something]
  replace: [tautulli]
```

## The toolkit

A plugin's default export is an integration, or a function that receives Valet's toolkit and returns one. The function form needs no imports.

```js title="data/integrations/hello.mjs"
export default ({ z, defineIntegration }) => defineIntegration({
  type: 'hello',
  name: 'Hello',
  config: z.object({ who: z.string().default('world') }),
  create: cfg => ({
    widgets: {
      greeting: {
        title: 'Hello',
        fetch: async () => ({ type: 'text', text: `Hello, ${cfg.who}!`, summary: { label: 'Hello', value: cfg.who } }),
      },
    },
  }),
});
```

| In the toolkit | What it is |
|---|---|
| `z` | Zod, the schema library. |
| `fmt` | The [formatters](/build/full/#formatting). |
| `defineIntegration` | The [full form](/build/full/). |
| `service` | The [short form](/build/service/). |
| `checkCard` | Checks a card against the catalog, for your own tests. |

The export can also be a list, for several integrations in one file.

`tally`, the recap helper, isn't in the toolkit. In a plugin, [write the slide out](/build/recap/#tally).

## What's checked

- A plugin must have `type`, `config` and `create`, or it's skipped with a message.
- A widget card that doesn't match the catalog becomes that widget's error, naming the field. The page doesn't break.
- A tool's bad card is dropped, the reason is logged, and the model still gets its `data`.

`checkCard` is strict: unknown fields are errors.

## Rules of the road

- Return cards from the [catalog](/cards/).
- Give every card a `summary`.
- Tools say what they need. Pick the narrowest `access`.
- Say what you're about to do, with [`confirm`](/build/confirm/).
- Pictures go through `ctx.image(ref)` and your [`image()`](/build/full/#images).

## Visuals of your own

The catalog covers most things, but a plugin can draw anything. Return a `showcase` card whose `visual.kind` is your plugin's name, and put a browser module beside it as `data/integrations/<kind>.web.js`.

```js title="data/integrations/my-thing.web.js"
export default function mount(box, data, { run }) {
  // draw into box: plain DOM, canvas, SVG
  // run(action, args) calls one of your actions
  return {
    update(data) { /* new data arrived */ },
    destroy() { /* the card went away */ },
  };
}
```

It's the same contract as Valet's own 3D models. Use the page's CSS variables, such as `var(--foreground)`, `var(--good)`, `var(--primary)` and `var(--muted-foreground)`, so it fits light and dark.

In chat, the assistant shows your visual whenever one of your tools returns that card.

`new-integration my-thing --full` writes a working one to start from.

## Cards for the house

Three cards draw their own glass and fill whatever row they land in. See [forecast](/cards/forecast/), [calendar](/cards/calendar/) and [thermostat](/cards/thermostat/).

A thermostat's buttons are your own actions, run like any other, so the same permissions apply. `set` names the action for a new target, and it's called with `{ temperature }`. The dial moves at once and sends one request when you let go, then waits for your next card to agree. So return the new `target` on the next fetch.

## Sharing one

Publish the file anywhere. If it's a good fit for everyone, move a `service()` into a family file in `src/integrations/services/` and open a pull request.
